claim_verdicts.evidence: webapplication10.md (moniker ">= aspnetcore-10.0"): "WebApplication.CreateBuilder initializes a new instance of the WebApplicationBuilder class with preconfigured defaults". Repo stage-1 Program.cs:10 `var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);` and lines 13-50 use `builder.Services.*` and `builder.Configuration[...]` on that object, so "registers its services and configuration on" matches the code as well as the docs.

Program.cs@stage-1: line 52 `var app = builder.Build();`, line 74 (last line) `app.Run();`. Execution this session (`docker compose up -d api`): log "Now listening on: http://[::]:8080" then "Application started. Press Ctrl+C to shut down."; every curl answered with header `Server: Kestrel`. fundamentals/servers/index.md:25 "Kestrel server is the default, cross-platform HTTP server implementation." fundamentals/host/web-host.md:440 "The `Run` method starts the web app and blocks the calling thread until the host is shut down".

Execution: swapped `AddProblemDetails()`<->`AddControllers()` and `AddSingleton<JwtTokenService>()`<->`AddScoped<OrderService>()`, then `docker compose up -d --build api`. Responses were identical apart from traceId: GET /api/v1/products 200, 421 bytes both times; GET /api/v1/nope 404 and POST /api/v1/products 405 with 0-byte bodies; POST /api/v1/auth/login {} -> same application/problem+json body. Docs: service-registration.md:78 "The single IMessageWriter is the last implementation to be registered" - order decides only among registrations of the same service type.

Endpoints are defined in the app and configured when the app starts." Execution: GET /api/v1/products -> 200; POST /api/v1/products -> 405 with `Allow: GET`, i.e. one pair per attribute-routed method.

claim_verdicts.source: run in examples/don-hang@stage-1; docker compose logs api

claim_verdicts.evidence: `git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Program.cs | cat -n`: line 52 `var app = builder.Build();`; line 74, the last line of the file, `app.Run();`. Between them: the `// lesson: backend.l1.migrations` block (`using (var scope = app.Services.CreateScope())` ... `context.Database.Migrate();`) and lines 67-72 `app.UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>(); ... app.UseAuthorization(); app.MapControllers();`. The lesson's block quotes lines 52-74 verbatim.

Execution against the stage-1 lab (db+api+lab+web up): `curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products` twice returned 200 with the same 421-byte JSON list starting [{"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000},...]. api log shows one "GET /api/v1/products responded 200 in ...ms" line per call (708ms, then 118ms, then 19ms), and with the temporary Console.WriteLine each call added exactly one "list ran" - computed per request, not cached from startup.

issues.quote: then restart the app once and watch its startup log
issues.text: The api runs from an image built by DonHang.Api/Dockerfile (`COPY DonHang.Api/ DonHang.Api/` then `RUN dotnet publish ...`), so a plain restart runs the old binary and never sees the edit. Executed: after adding the Console.WriteLine and `docker compose restart api`, "list ran" appeared neither at startup nor after two curls (grep count 0) - the promised "Both curls do print it, once each" does not happen. After `docker compose up -d --build api` the same steps gave 0 at startup and exactly 2 after the curls. The lesson also never says how to read the app's log.
issues.fix: Step 1: "... then rebuild and restart the app with `docker compose up -d --build api` from the repo root, and watch `docker compose logs api`." Step 2: "Once the startup lines end with no such line printed, run `curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products` twice and look at `docker compose logs api` again." Keep the expected result as written; it is exactly what the rebuild produces.

issues.quote: A method is attribute-routed when the method and its class carry attributes stating the HTTP method and the path
issues.text: Unlisted claim (nothing in .meta.json covers the definition of attribute-routed) and wrong as a general rule: the route template may sit entirely on the action, with no attribute on the class. The docs sample for attribute routing is `public class HomeController : Controller` with `[Route("")] [Route("Index")] [Route("/")]` on the methods only; routing.md:425 "Route templates that you apply to an action and that begin with `/` or `~/` don't get combined with route templates that you apply to the controller."
issues.fix: Write it as a description of this code, not a definition: "A method is attribute-routed when attributes state the HTTP method and the path right next to the code itself - in `ProductsController` the attribute on the class carries the path and the attribute on each method carries the HTTP method." Add the sentence to .meta.json claims (kind behavior, version_key aspnetcore).

issues.quote: the order between them only decides what is available to the app, not how a later request is answered
issues.text: As written the subject is "the order", so the sentence says the order decides what is available to the app. It does not: both registrations end up available whichever order they are written in. Claim 3 in the ledger only covers the second half ("does not affect how any individual request is later handled"), so the first half is an unlisted and incorrect statement that a junior can read as "order controls availability".
issues.fix: Rewrite: "When two calls register different things, as every call in this file does, the order between them decides nothing: both are available to the app either way, and neither order changes how a later request is answered." Check the same wording in the five-line summary item 2, which is already correct.

issues.quote: False, because `OrderService` and `JwtTokenService` are unrelated to `/api/v1/products` entirely.
issues.text: Option d is true of the repo: `ProductsController(DonHangDbContext db)` takes only the DbContext, and neither OrderService nor JwtTokenService takes any part in answering GET /api/v1/products. Two options (c and d) are therefore defensible for a reader who has read the code, and d's explanation rebuts a different statement ("Both lines are in Program.cs because the app needs both") - unrelated to the app is not what d says.
issues.fix: Give d a reason that is actually false, e.g. en: "False, because ASP.NET Core sorts the `Services.Add...` calls itself before the app starts, so the order they are written in is never used" (vi likewise), and change explanation.d to: "Nothing sorts or rewrites the registrations; they stay in the order written - the order simply has no effect on how a request is handled."

issues.quote: is what makes an **endpoint** exist at all
issues.text: True of this file (MapControllers is Program.cs's only endpoint-creating call), but phrased as a general rule it tells a junior that endpoints can only come from MapControllers. fundamentals/routing.md:80-83 lists MapRazorPages, MapControllers, MapHub<THub> and MapGrpcService<TService> as the calls that create endpoints.
issues.fix: Scope it to this app: "One of those wiring calls, `app.MapControllers()`, is what makes this app's **endpoint**s exist at all" (quiz q3 already scopes it correctly with "The one call in `DonHang.Api/Program.cs`").

issues.quote: register a database connection, a standard error format (`AddProblemDetails()`), an order service, and a way to issue tokens
issues.text: `AddDonHangInfrastructure(connectionString)` adds more than "a database connection": DonHang.Infrastructure/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs@stage-1 registers `AddDbContext<DonHangDbContext>(options => options.UseNpgsql(connectionString))`, `IOrderRepository -> EfOrderRepository` and `INotifier -> LoggingNotifier`. The list reads as one line = one thing, which is the undercount the previous round set out to fix.
issues.fix: Say what the line is without counting its contents: "... register the app's database access (that one call adds the database context and the classes built on it), a standard error format (`AddProblemDetails()`), an order service, and a way to issue tokens."

issues.quote: turns each attribute-routed method on them into a method-and-path pair Kestrel can route a matching request to
issues.text: I know what a C# attribute is, but "attribute-routed" is new and never explained. Which attribute? Where does the path text live? This is the one sentence that is supposed to tell me how a method gets tied to `/api/v1/products`, and I have to take it on faith. No controller code appears anywhere in the lesson, so I cannot look it up myself.
issues.fix: In Core concepts, after the `endpoint` bullet, add one sentence: "A method is attribute-routed when the method and its class carry attributes that state the HTTP method and the path, so the pair is written next to the code itself." Then the two later uses of the word are readable.

issues.quote: it looks at classes like `ProductsController` and turns each attribute-routed method on them into a method-and-path pair
issues.text: "classes like `ProductsController`" assumes I know what a controller is. Nothing in what I have been taught says a controller is a class whose methods answer requests, and the lesson never says it either — yet `AddControllers()`, `MapControllers()` and `ProductsController` all depend on it, and the quiz asks about a method "inside `ProductsController`".
issues.fix: In the same sentence, gloss it once: "...classes like `ProductsController` — classes whose methods are written to answer requests — and turns each...".

issues.quote: You do not see a URL anywhere near it. Where does an ASP.NET Core app actually start, and how does one line connect to a specific path?
issues.text: The first half of the question is answered well. The second half is not: I finish the lesson still not seeing where `/api/v1/products` is written. The answer given is "MapControllers turns attribute-routed methods into method-and-path pairs", which just moves my question one step back — I still do not know what states the path, and my teammate's claim is never actually confirmed or explained.
issues.fix: In section 4, after the `app.MapControllers()` paragraph, add one sentence closing the loop: "That is why your teammate could point at `app.MapControllers()`: the path `/api/v1/products` is written on `ProductsController` itself, and this line is what makes the app notice it."

issues.text: The diagram shows "wiring calls" and "MapControllers" as two separate steps, one after the other, so I read it as: first the wiring calls happen, then MapControllers happens. The prose then says "One of those wiring calls, `app.MapControllers()`" — so it is inside the box before it, not after it. I had to stop and decide which one to believe.
issues.fix: Relabel node E so the diagram matches the prose, e.g. `D[wiring calls] --> E[... incl. MapControllers]`, or drop node E and mention MapControllers only in the prose.

issues.quote:
// lesson: backend.l1.migrations
// Applies pending migrations on start, so a fresh `db` container ends up on
issues.text: The second code block is 23 lines and its own comments use migrations, `dotnet ef database update`, `db` container, schema, middleware, order-matters, auth, routing, CORS — none of which I know. I read all of them before the prose underneath told me "Read only the first and last lines for now". By then I had already lost the thread and assumed I was missing a prerequisite.
issues.fix: Move that instruction above the block: replace the intro sentence with "`Build()` and `Run()` sit at the two ends of a longer block — read only its first and last lines for now; everything between them, comments included, belongs to later lessons."

issues.quote: the rest register a database connection, an order service, and a way to issue tokens
issues.text: I counted: after `AddControllers()` the block has `AddProblemDetails()`, a `connectionString` variable with a `?? throw`, `AddDonHangInfrastructure(...)`, `AddScoped<OrderService>()` and `AddSingleton<JwtTokenService>()`. That is five things, and "the rest" names only three. I spent time trying to work out which one `AddProblemDetails()` is supposed to be, and whether the `?? throw` line counts as a registration.
issues.fix: Make the count match, e.g.: "...the rest read the database connection string and register a database connection, a standard error format, an order service, and a way to issue tokens."

issues.quote: both calls print the same product list, computed fresh each time by that method — nothing about that list was computed back when `app.MapControllers()` itself ran
issues.text: Two identical outputs are exactly what I would expect if the list had been computed once at startup and kept (I know what a cache is). The exercise tells me to conclude the opposite from an observation that cannot show it. Step 1, "find the line in the quoted block above", also produces nothing I can see; the whole conclusion rests on trusting the text.
issues.fix: Make step 2 show something startup could not have produced: have the reader add a `Console.WriteLine` inside the method (as quiz q5 already describes), restart once, watch the startup log stay silent, then curl twice and see the line print twice. State that as the Expected result.

issues.quote: You notice this when reordering a wiring line changes what a request sees, and reordering a `Services.Add` line does not.
issues.text: Section 5 told me the wiring lines belong to another lesson and to skip them; here I am told I would notice something by reordering exactly those lines. I do not know what any of them does, so I cannot picture what "changes what a request sees" would look like — the correction asks me to trust a result I have no way to predict.
issues.fix: Replace the "You notice this" sentence with one I can check today: "You notice this the first time a request behaves differently after a wiring line moves — which is what the next lesson is about."

issues.text: "wiring calls" is a phrase the lesson invents. In the diagram it appears as a labelled box before any prose has said what it means; I only got a working meaning two paragraphs later ("Program.cs wires up the steps every incoming request will pass through"). Reading the diagram first, I had no idea what that node stood for.
issues.fix: Add a Core concepts bullet or a one-line gloss right under the diagram: "wiring calls — the `app.Use...` / `app.Map...` lines between `Build()` and `Run()` that set up what every request passes through."

issues.quote: The `WebApplication` object, the same one `Run()` is later called on to start Kestrel
issues.text: The correct option is almost word-for-word the Core concepts bullet ("what `builder.Build()` produces; ... the object whose `Run()` call starts Kestrel"), and it is also by far the longest of the four. I could pick it by matching the wording and by length alone, without having understood the two phases.
issues.fix: Shorten option a to "The `WebApplication` object that `Run()` is later called on" and lengthen one distractor, e.g. option c -> "A new database connection, opened from the registered connection string and ready to run queries".

issues.quote: `OrderService` is used by the code behind `/api/v1/orders`, so the two lines are related — just not in a way that reordering affects.
issues.text: Nothing in the lesson says there is an `/api/v1/orders` path or that `OrderService` sits behind it — the only path I was shown is `/api/v1/products`. The same goes for `AddScoped` vs `AddSingleton` in the question, and for `UseCors` / `RequestLoggingMiddleware` in q6. I can still answer, but each of these made me stop and check whether I had missed a paragraph.
issues.fix: Use the path and names the lesson actually shows: ask q2 about a later request to `/api/v1/products`, and drop the claim about what `OrderService` is used by from option d's explanation.

issues.quote: Everything an ASP.NET Core app needs before it can run — a database connection, a way to issue tokens, and so on — gets registered on that one object, and the order these registrations happen in does not decide how a later request is answered; it only decides what is available for the app to use.
issues.text: One sentence carrying an aside, a negative claim and its correction, split by a dash pair and a semicolon. I lost the subject halfway and had to read it twice to see that "the order ... does not decide" was a new idea and not part of the list.
issues.fix: Split after "gets registered on that one object." Start a new sentence: "The order these registrations happen in does not decide how a later request is answered; it only decides what is available for the app to use."
